modules.title: Introduction: Formulation of the problem
modules.hook: The same congenital lesion can behave differently in a fetus, a newborn and an adult. Begin with anatomy and physiology, then predict the findings.
modules.audience: Pediatric residents, cardiology trainees and clinicians studying congenital heart disease from infancy to adulthood
modules.prerequisites: Core cardiovascular anatomy and physiology; chapters1–2 introduce the diagnostic approach and functional murmurs.
modules.estimated_minutes_note: Planning estimate for five units and feedback; full reference reading takes longer.

lessons.objective: Explain why congenital heart disease is a life-course condition
lessons.title: A changing condition
lessons.text: Congenital anatomy can acquire changing physiologic expression over time. A congenital malformation may evolve during gestation and extrauterine life; a bicuspid valve can become stenotic decades after birth.

lessons.objective: Recognize that important congenital disorders may be electrical
lessons.title: Beyond visible malformation
lessons.text: Congenital functional abnormalities can exist without a gross structural defect. The source includes congenital complete heart block among functionally significant conditions that need not be gross structural defects.

lessons.objective: Relate postnatal pulmonary adaptation to changing shunt physiology
lessons.title: Birth changes the physiology
lessons.text: Lung expansion and falling pulmonary vascular resistance redistribute flow. Lung expansion, rising oxygen tension, reduced pulmonary resistance and elimination of the placental circulation substantially alter cardiovascular physiology.

lessons.objective: Combine bedside observations and imaging in diagnostic reasoning
lessons.title: Clinical synthesis
lessons.text: Integrate the imaging with prior clinical observations and predicted physiology. The diagnostic approach synthesizes history, examination, ECG, radiography and advanced imaging into a coherent anatomic–physiologic explanation.

lessons.objective: Adapt the order of assessment while preserving diagnostic synthesis
lessons.title: Flexible examination sequence
lessons.text: Examine while calm and integrate the history and other findings afterward. The depth and synthesis of analysis matter more than a rigid order; examining an infant during a calm interval may improve the assessment.

modules.title: Functional murmurs
modules.hook: A murmur is a finding to explain, not a diagnosis. Use its timing, location, quality, context and response to position before assigning a cause.
modules.audience: Pediatric residents, cardiology trainees and clinicians studying congenital heart disease from infancy to adulthood
modules.prerequisites: Core cardiovascular anatomy and physiology; chapters1–2 introduce the diagnostic approach and functional murmurs.
modules.estimated_minutes_note: Planning estimate for five units and feedback; full reference reading takes longer.

lessons.objective: Recognize the typical clinical pattern of a Still murmur
lessons.title: The vibratory childhood murmur
lessons.text: A Still murmur. The typical Still murmur is vibratory or buzzing, midsystolic and most prominent between the apex and lower left sternal edge in the supine child.

lessons.objective: Recognize the distribution and interpretive limits of neonatal branch pulmonary murmurs
lessons.title: Transient branch pulmonary flow
lessons.text: Transient disparity between the pulmonary trunk and its branch sizes. The neonatal pulmonary trunk–branch size disparity and branch geometry can produce widely transmitted systolic turbulence; the murmur alone does not distinguish transient physiology from fixed branch stenosis.

lessons.objective: Distinguish a venous hum from other continuous murmurs
lessons.title: Position-dependent continuous sound
lessons.text: A cervical venous hum. Recumbency, neutral neck position and reduced jugular flow can diminish or abolish the venous hum.

lessons.objective: Recognize the localization and shoulder response of an arterial supraclavicular murmur
lessons.title: Supraclavicular arterial origin
lessons.text: Flow vibrations near the origins of the major brachiocephalic arteries. The supraclavicular arterial murmur is systolic, maximal above the clavicles and may diminish or disappear with shoulder hyperextension.

lessons.objective: Evaluate the proposed relationship between ventricular bands and a Still murmur
lessons.title: Association is not a settled mechanism
lessons.text: Band prevalence persists across ages while Still murmur prevalence falls toward adolescence. The mismatch between age-related murmur prevalence and band prevalence, and the source’s explicit uncertainty, prevent treating the association as a settled universal mechanism.

case.intro: A fictional 7-year-old is referred after a murmur is heard during a routine visit. Exercise tolerance, pulses and oxygenation are normal.

stages.information: The sound is vibratory and midsystolic, loudest between the apex and lower left sternal edge when the child is supine. Other heart sounds are normal.
stages.prompt: Which source-described pattern best fits this sound?
options: A Still murmur
A purely diastolic regurgitant murmur
A cervical venous hum
A continuous ductal murmur
stages.feedback: A vibratory midsystolic sound in this location and context is the characteristic Still pattern. The interpretation still uses the whole clinical assessment.

stages.information: A separate continuous sound is then heard above the right clavicle while sitting upright. It disappears with recumbency; it is distinct from the original precordial systolic sound.
stages.prompt: How should this second sound be interpreted?
options: A venous hum can coexist as a separate functional flow sound
Every continuous sound establishes a patent ductus
The systolic sound has necessarily become a diastolic valve lesion
The new sound proves the earlier examination was impossible
stages.feedback: A supraclavicular continuous sound with this positional behavior fits a venous hum. Distinguishing the two sounds avoids forcing separate observations into one incorrect mechanism.

stages.information: Imaging obtained during the referral shows no important structural defect and an incidental left ventricular band. A learner claims this proves the cause of every Still murmur.
stages.prompt: Which explanation best respects the source evidence?
options: Every ventricular band is an obstructive valve lesion
The association does not establish a universal mechanism
An incidental band makes the rest of the assessment irrelevant
All Still murmurs must disappear only after a band is removed
stages.feedback: The source explicitly leaves the mechanism unsettled and notes the mismatch between band prevalence and the age-related prevalence of the murmur. Association does not establish a necessary cause.

case.debrief: Describe timing, quality and distribution before assigning a mechanism. Positional behavior can help distinguish an additional venous hum. Do not convert an anatomic association into a universal causal explanation.

modules.title: The cardiac malpositions
modules.hook: A heart on the right does not tell you every chamber’s identity or connection. Describe position, situs and sequential segmental anatomy separately.
modules.audience: Pediatric residents, cardiology trainees and clinicians studying congenital heart disease from infancy to adulthood
modules.prerequisites: Core cardiovascular anatomy and physiology; chapters1–2 introduce the diagnostic approach and functional murmurs.
modules.estimated_minutes_note: Planning estimate for five units and feedback; full reference reading takes longer.

lessons.objective: Distinguish a secondary shift of the heart from an intrinsic positional arrangement
lessons.title: Position and displacement
lessons.text: Secondary cardiac displacement. Cardiac displacement is a secondary shift in intrathoracic position, such as one produced by diaphragmatic eventration.

lessons.objective: Trace cardiac components without substituting side labels for morphology
lessons.title: Sequential segmental analysis
lessons.text: Identify the atria, valves, ventricles and arterial connections systematically. The source describes systematic attention to morphology, atrioventricular connections, ventriculoarterial connections and great-artery relationships.

lessons.objective: Recognize the combined visceral and cardiac pattern of situs inversus with dextrocardia
lessons.title: Mirror-image arrangement
lessons.text: Situs inversus with dextrocardia. The described heart and abdominal viscera are in the mirror-image positions of the usual arrangement.

lessons.objective: Explain physiologic correction through atrioventricular and ventriculoarterial discordance
lessons.title: The effect of two discordant connections
lessons.text: Two discordant connections restore the appropriate destinations of blood. Atrioventricular and ventriculoarterial discordance can together produce physiologic correction of blood-flow destinations.

lessons.objective: Identify bilateral right-sided morphology without equating it with position alone
lessons.title: Isomerism is a morphologic descriptor
lessons.text: Right isomerism. Right isomerism describes bilateral morphologically right characteristics in structures normally different on the two sides.

case.intro: A fictional adult has an unusual cardiac position discovered during routine chest imaging. No anatomy or physiology is assumed from the word dextrocardia alone.

stages.information: The cardiac silhouette and stomach are on the right, and the liver is on the left.
stages.prompt: Which arrangement best describes these findings?
options: Bilateral left isomerism established by position alone
Situs inversus with dextrocardia
Situs inversus with levocardia
Situs solitus with levocardia
stages.feedback: Right thoracic cardiac position with reversed abdominal viscera is the source-described mirror-image arrangement. Isomerism requires morphologic assessment.

stages.information: A standard ECG shows inverted P waves in lead I and an upright P wave in aVR. The tracing is being interpreted for the first time.
stages.prompt: Which step belongs before interpreting these as pathologic electrical findings?
options: Ignore the cardiac position because every ECG has the same orientation
Declare atrial situs from one wave without checking technical placement
Verify lead attachment and interpret the tracing in the documented atrial and cardiac arrangement
Assume these findings establish myocardial infarction
stages.feedback: The source emphasizes checking lead attachment first. Mirror-image atrial depolarization changes expected limb-lead patterns, and interpretation depends on the documented situs.

stages.information: Echocardiography identifies a left-sided morphologic right atrium connected through a tricuspid valve to a morphologic right ventricle; the corresponding morphologic left chambers are on the right. Further arterial connections are traced directly.
stages.prompt: How should the atrioventricular connection be described?
options: A single-ventricle connection proven by the side labels
Morphologically concordant despite the reversed locations
Discordant solely because the right ventricle is left-sided
Undefined because position always replaces morphology
stages.feedback: Concordance describes the appropriate morphologic atrial–ventricular pairing, not whether a chamber occupies a familiar side of the chest. Continue tracing the arterial connections rather than assuming them.

case.debrief: Describe position and visceral situs, check ECG technique, then identify morphology and trace connections. A side label is not a substitute for segmental anatomy or its resulting physiology.

modules.title: Isolated congenital complete heart block
modules.hook: A slow pulse can reveal an electrical problem even when cardiac anatomy appears normal. Link the venous pulse and heart sounds to the ECG.
modules.audience: Pediatric residents, cardiology trainees and clinicians studying congenital heart disease from infancy to adulthood
modules.prerequisites: Core cardiovascular anatomy and physiology; chapters1–2 introduce the diagnostic approach and functional murmurs.
modules.estimated_minutes_note: Planning estimate for five units and feedback; full reference reading takes longer.

lessons.objective: Describe a source-supported mechanism of isolated congenital heart block
lessons.title: Passive autoimmunity
lessons.text: Transplacental transfer of maternal IgG with injury to fetal conduction tissue. The source describes passive autoimmunity involving maternal IgG antibodies, including Ro/SSA and La/SSB associations; maternal lupus can become apparent only later.

lessons.objective: Recognize the ECG relationship in complete atrioventricular block
lessons.title: Electrical independence
lessons.text: Atrial and ventricular activation are independent. In complete heart block, P waves and QRS complexes occur independently, rather than maintaining a fixed conducted relationship.

lessons.objective: Explain intermittent large jugular A waves in atrioventricular dissociation
lessons.title: Cannon venous waves
lessons.text: Right atrial contraction against a closed tricuspid valve. Independent atrial and ventricular activity can bring atrial contraction against the closed tricuspid valve, abruptly amplifying the venous A wave.

lessons.objective: Relate changing atrioventricular timing to variable first-sound intensity
lessons.title: Variable first heart sound
lessons.text: The changing atrial–ventricular timing alters valve position at ventricular systole. Because atria and ventricles beat independently, the PR relationship changes and first-sound intensity can vary widely.

lessons.objective: Choose the appropriate test when conduction disease is suspected
lessons.title: Normal radiography does not exclude block
lessons.text: Assess the atrial–ventricular relationship on a standard ECG. The radiographic appearance can be normal; the source emphasizes the standard ECG for establishing complete heart block.

case.intro: A fictional child is followed from fetal recognition of bradycardia into childhood. The case teaches source-edition mechanisms and recognition rather than a pacing or resuscitation protocol.

stages.information: Fetal assessment identifies persistent bradycardia and no major structural malformation. Maternal testing identifies anti-Ro/SSA antibodies despite no established clinical diagnosis of lupus.
stages.prompt: Which mechanism should be considered?
options: Direct transmission of the maternal cardiac rhythm
Exclusion of immune injury because maternal lupus is not clinically established
Passive immune injury from transplacental maternal IgG
The need for a gross ventricular septal defect before conduction disease can occur
stages.feedback: The source describes maternal antibody-mediated fetal conduction injury and notes that overt maternal lupus may not be apparent at the time of the infant’s diagnosis.

stages.information: After birth, the ECG records independent atrial P waves and a slower regular ventricular rhythm with narrow QRS complexes.
stages.prompt: Which interpretation best explains the electrical relationship?
options: A fixed 2:1 conducted rhythm established by the description
A structural shunt diagnosed from the QRS width alone
Physiologic sinus bradycardia with an intact fixed PR relationship
Complete atrioventricular block with an independent escape rhythm
stages.feedback: Independent P waves and QRS complexes establish atrioventricular dissociation. The common narrow complex reflects the usual activation pattern but is interpreted within the complete tracing.

stages.information: Years later, after a largely asymptomatic interval, the child develops an unexplained syncopal episode.
stages.prompt: Which conclusion is most appropriate?
options: Use one age-independent pulse cutoff as a complete management plan
Assume congenital block can never cause symptoms in children
Reassess rhythm and hemodynamic status; prior symptom-free periods do not establish permanent stability
Exclude an arrhythmic cause because the prior chest radiograph was normal
stages.feedback: The source describes Stokes–Adams episodes and serious rhythm-related events even in previously asymptomatic young patients. Assessment must consider the rhythm, ventricular function and clinical presentation.

case.debrief: An apparently normal structure does not establish normal conduction. Connect maternal antibody exposure, ECG evidence and later symptoms without substituting this teaching scenario for individual clinical assessment.

modules.title: Congenital abnormalities of the pericardium
modules.hook: An unusual cardiac silhouette may reflect its pericardial support rather than a primary chamber lesion. Relate the radiograph to motion and cross-sectional anatomy.

lessons.objective: Recognize the source-described radiographic clue to partial left pericardial absence
lessons.title: A focal left-border bulge
lessons.text: Herniation of the left atrial appendage through a partial left pericardial defect. Partial absence of the left pericardium may permit left atrial appendage herniation, producing the described convex left-border shadow.

lessons.objective: Recognize displacement and lung interposition in complete pericardial absence
lessons.title: Mobility with complete absence
lessons.text: Loss of normal pericardial restraint. Complete absence can produce striking cardiac mobility, leftward/posterior displacement and interposed lung tissue.

lessons.objective: Distinguish suggestive echocardiographic findings from definitive cross-sectional assessment
lessons.title: Confirm the anatomy
lessons.text: Thoracic CT or cardiac MRI. The source identifies CT and MRI as definitive modalities; echocardiography may suggest complete absence and identify coexisting defects.

lessons.objective: Recognize the typical radiographic location of a congenital pericardial cyst
lessons.title: A cardiophrenic cyst pattern
lessons.text: A congenital pericardial cyst. A congenital pericardial cyst typically forms a smooth homogeneous density at the right cardiophrenic angle.

lessons.objective: Explain right-sided chamber enlargement in the absence of normal pericardial constraint
lessons.title: Constraint and right-sided dimensions
lessons.text: Reduced pericardial restraint particularly affects the relatively thin-walled right-sided chambers. Loss of normal pericardial constraint particularly affects the right ventricle and right atrium and can alter systemic venous return and septal motion.

modules.title: Congenitally corrected transposition of the great arteries
modules.hook: A circulation can be physiologically in series while its valves, ventricles and conduction system remain abnormal.
modules.audience: Pediatric residents, cardiology trainees and clinicians studying congenital heart disease from infancy to adulthood
modules.prerequisites: Core cardiovascular anatomy and physiology; chapters1–2 introduce the diagnostic approach and functional murmurs.
modules.estimated_minutes_note: Planning estimate for five units and feedback; full reference reading takes longer.

lessons.objective: Trace blood through discordant atrioventricular and arterial connections
lessons.title: Double discordance
lessons.text: Atrioventricular and ventriculoarterial discordance. Two discordant junctions place systemic venous blood in the pulmonary circuit and pulmonary venous blood in the systemic circuit, so the circulations are in series.

lessons.objective: Explain why an anatomically corrected circulation remains vulnerable
lessons.title: Systemic ventricular burden
lessons.text: The systemic morphologic right ventricle must sustain a workload for which its usual geometry and blood supply are not designed. The systemic right ventricle retains right-ventricular geometry and a morphologically right coronary supply despite systemic loading.

lessons.objective: Identify the valve responsible for left-sided atrioventricular regurgitation
lessons.title: Systemic atrioventricular valve
lessons.text: Morphologic tricuspid valve. The inverted left atrioventricular valve is morphologically tricuspid; Ebstein-like abnormalities and age-related regurgitation are important.

lessons.objective: Explain an age-related substrate for atrioventricular block
lessons.title: Progressive conduction disease
lessons.text: Replacement of conduction fibers by fibrous tissue in the long penetrating bundle. Fibrous replacement in the long penetrating bundle contributes to age-related atrioventricular block; defects may occur at several conduction levels.

lessons.objective: Interpret the characteristic precordial Q-wave pattern
lessons.title: Reversed septal activation
lessons.text: Q waves in right precordial leads with absent left precordial Q waves. Inverted bundle branches activate the septum from right to left, reversing the usual precordial septal Q-wave pattern.

case.intro: Fictional teaching scenario: a previously well adult is evaluated for an unusual second heart sound.

stages.information: A loud second sound is heard at the left base. The anatomy and pulmonary pressure have not yet been established.
stages.prompt: What interpretive caution is appropriate?
options: Exclude a congenital connection abnormality because the adult is well
Diagnose pulmonary hypertension from the sound alone
Do not infer pulmonary hypertension from loudness alone; an anterior aortic valve can produce this finding
Assume the loud component must arise from a posterior pulmonary valve
stages.feedback: An anterior aortic valve may produce a loud basal second sound that is mistaken for pulmonary hypertension.

stages.information: The ECG now shows Q waves in right precordial leads with absent left precordial Q waves.
stages.prompt: Which mechanism should be considered?
options: Normal left-to-right septal activation
Atrial activation as the source of septal Q waves
Reversed septal activation associated with ventricular inversion
Pulmonary pressure alone as proof of the Q-wave distribution
stages.feedback: Right-to-left septal activation with inverted bundle branches reverses the usual precordial Q-wave pattern.

stages.information: Echocardiography shows right atrium–morphologic left ventricle–pulmonary trunk and left atrium–morphologic right ventricle–aorta.
stages.prompt: What explains the absence of obligatory parallel-circulation physiology?
options: Both junctions are discordant, placing the circuits in series
Only the arterial connection is discordant
Concordance at both junctions
A single ventricle necessarily mixes all venous returns
stages.feedback: Double discordance redirects each venous stream to its appropriate circulation, despite abnormal segmental connections.

case.debrief: Interpret the sound cautiously, use the ECG as an anatomic clue, and confirm segmental connections by imaging. Physiologic correction does not establish normal systemic ventricular or valve function.

modules.hook: The site of obstruction, valve mobility and the time course of regurgitation change the diagnostic signs.

lessons.objective: Use an aortic ejection sound to localize mobile valvar obstruction
lessons.title: Localizing an ejection sound
lessons.text: A mobile stenotic aortic valve. The sound arises from abrupt movement of a mobile doming valve and identifies valvar level rather than degree.

lessons.objective: Avoid equating lower murmur intensity with improvement
lessons.title: A quiet murmur in ventricular failure
lessons.text: Reduced murmur intensity does not establish reduced obstruction. Aortic stenosis murmur intensity can decrease in left ventricular failure; loudness is not a stand-alone measure of obstruction.

lessons.objective: Resolve a misleading false raphe on echocardiography
lessons.title: Imaging a bicuspid valve
lessons.text: Image the open valve for two unequal doming leaflets and an elliptical orifice. Open-valve imaging reveals the bicuspid anatomy that can be obscured by a false raphe during closure.

lessons.objective: Recognize the chronic severe aortic regurgitation pulse pattern
lessons.title: Chronic regurgitant pulse
lessons.text: Rapid rise, wide pulse pressure and brisk collapse. Chronic severe regurgitation produces a rapid upstroke, wide pulse pressure, sometimes a bisferiens peak, and brisk collapse.

lessons.objective: Distinguish acute severe regurgitation from the chronic bedside pattern
lessons.title: Acute regurgitation can sound soft
lessons.text: Relatively low regurgitant flow velocity can make severe acute disease acoustically unimpressive. The source describes short, medium-pitched, disarmingly soft murmurs in acute severe regurgitation; chronic peripheral signs may be absent.

modules.title: Coarctation of the aorta and interrupted aortic arch
modules.hook: A routine arm-and-leg pulse comparison can reveal an obstructive lesion that a quiet anterior chest examination misses.
modules.audience: Pediatric residents, cardiology trainees and clinicians studying congenital heart disease from infancy to adulthood
modules.prerequisites: Core cardiovascular anatomy and physiology; chapters1–2 introduce the diagnostic approach and functional murmurs.
modules.estimated_minutes_note: Planning estimate for five units and feedback; full reference reading takes longer.

lessons.objective: Select a focused bedside screen for coarctation
lessons.title: Arm–leg examination
lessons.text: Compare upper-extremity and femoral pulses and blood pressures. Upper–lower extremity pulse and pressure differences are hallmarks; brachial–femoral comparison is particularly practical in infants.

lessons.objective: Explain why obstruction alone does not capture coarctation physiology
lessons.title: Vascular contribution to hypertension
lessons.text: A stiff, poorly distensible precoarctation aorta. Increased collagen and reduced smooth muscle stiffen the proximal aorta, contributing to systolic hypertension and baroreceptor resetting.

lessons.objective: Interpret absent rib notching in a young child
lessons.title: Age and collateral signs
lessons.text: Notching usually develops later through enlarged posterior intercostal collateral arteries. Collateral posterior intercostal arteries produce notching, which seldom appears before age six years.

lessons.objective: Relate neonatal deterioration to ductal constriction
lessons.title: Ductal closure and neonatal presentation
lessons.text: Closure of the ductus arteriosus. The source specifically associates acute neonatal symptoms in severe coarctation with ductal closure.

lessons.objective: Explain maintained femoral pulses before ductal constriction
lessons.title: Distal perfusion in interrupted arch
lessons.text: Pulmonary trunk through a patent ductus into the descending aorta. Pulmonary trunk–ductus–descending aortic continuity can supply the lower body; diminishing femoral pulses can signal ductal constriction.

case.intro: Fictional teaching scenario: an infant deteriorates after an initially reassuring newborn period.

stages.information: The infant develops tachypnea and poor perfusion; no prominent anterior murmur is heard.
stages.prompt: Which bedside assessment remains important?
options: Use carotid pulsation alone to exclude obstruction
Exclude arch obstruction because the murmur is quiet
Compare brachial and femoral pulses and upper–lower extremity pressures
Wait for rib notching to develop
stages.feedback: Pulse and pressure comparison directly investigates an obstructive systemic arterial lesion even when auscultation is unimpressive.

stages.information: Femoral pulses are reduced, and the timing of deterioration coincides with ductal constriction.
stages.prompt: Which physiologic interpretation is supported?
options: Mature collateral circulation is required before symptoms
Loss of ductal support can unmask severe neonatal aortic obstruction
Ductal closure has no relevance to systemic obstruction
A normal anterior examination excludes a hemodynamic lesion
stages.feedback: Severe coarctation may become acutely symptomatic as the ductus closes; anatomy must be established rather than inferred from the murmur.

stages.information: Imaging demonstrates an interrupted arch and a pulmonary trunk–ductus–descending aortic pathway.
stages.prompt: How were lower-body pulses maintained before further ductal constriction?
options: Flow across a normally continuous arch
Direct pulmonary venous flow to the femoral artery
Ductal delivery of pulmonary arterial blood into the descending aorta
Rib collateral circulation as the only possible neonatal route
stages.feedback: That arterial pathway can maintain distal flow temporarily; femoral pulses decline as the ductus constricts.

case.debrief: A quiet murmur does not settle the diagnosis. Connect age, pulse distribution and ductal physiology, then establish the precise arch anatomy. This case provides no drug dose or definitive management protocol.

modules.title: Congenital obstruction to left atrial flow: Mitral stenosis, cor triatriatum, pulmonary vein stenosis
modules.hook: Similar pulmonary venous congestion can arise from obstruction at several levels before left ventricular filling.

lessons.objective: Recognize the defining papillary muscle arrangement
lessons.title: Parachute apparatus
lessons.text: Parachute mitral valve. A single papillary muscle receiving all chordae defines the parachute arrangement and can restrict interchordal flow.

lessons.objective: Identify the obstructive components of Shone complex
lessons.title: Associated left-sided obstruction
lessons.text: Supravalvular mitral ring, parachute mitral valve, subaortic stenosis and coarctation. The classic four lesions are left-sided inflow/outflow obstructions; not all need be present or functionally significant.

lessons.objective: Explain why congenital stenosis need not sound rheumatic
lessons.title: An absent opening snap
lessons.text: The abnormal leaflet apparatus may not make the brisk opening and closing movements required for those sounds. The characteristic brisk motion of a mobile anterior leaflet is not a feature of the congenital lesion described.

lessons.objective: Differentiate cor triatriatum from a supravalvular mitral ring
lessons.title: Membrane position
lessons.text: Cor triatriatum. A membrane proximal to the appendage and valve distinguishes typical cor triatriatum from a supravalvular ring.

lessons.objective: Localize obstruction proximal to a normal-sized left atrium
lessons.title: Regional pulmonary venous congestion
lessons.text: Unequal stenosis of individual pulmonary veins proximal to the left atrium. Individual veins can have different severities of narrowing, producing regional congestion while the downstream left atrium remains normal-sized.

modules.hook: Obstruction above, at or below the pulmonary valve produces different sounds despite sharing right-ventricular pressure loading.

lessons.objective: Distinguish dysplastic from mobile dome-shaped pulmonary stenosis
lessons.title: Valve morphology
lessons.text: Dysplastic pulmonary valve stenosis. Dysplastic pulmonary stenosis has thickened separate poorly mobile leaflets without commissural fusion.

lessons.objective: Recognize a distinctive pulmonary valvar ejection sound
lessons.title: Respiratory ejection-click behavior
lessons.text: Reduced additional cephalad movement of a mobile pulmonary valve during ventricular contraction. Inspiration prepositions the mobile valve cephalad through increased right atrial contraction, reducing further excursion and the ejection sound.

lessons.objective: Avoid using murmur loudness alone to exclude severe neonatal stenosis
lessons.title: Critical obstruction with a soft murmur
lessons.text: Pinpoint pulmonary stenosis can have a deceptively soft murmur. The source emphasizes that pinpoint neonatal stenosis may sound disarmingly soft despite severe obstruction.

lessons.objective: Explain preserved P2 intensity in pulmonary arterial stenosis
lessons.title: Branch stenosis and the second sound
lessons.text: The central pulmonary diastolic pressure can remain normal or nearly normal at valve closure. Branch stenosis can raise central systolic pressure while pressure falls to near-normal diastolic levels, so valve closure need not be accentuated.

lessons.objective: Recognize the described isolated congenital pulmonary regurgitation pattern
lessons.title: Low-pressure regurgitant sound
lessons.text: Short delayed low-to-medium-frequency crescendo-decrescendo murmur at the upper left sternal border. The source describes a distinctive short delayed low-to-medium-frequency diastolic murmur, sometimes louder with inspiration.

modules.title: Ebstein’s anomaly of the tricuspid valve
modules.hook: The effective right ventricle, atrialized segment and interatrial pathway determine more than the apparent size of the heart.

lessons.objective: Identify the morphologic partition created by displaced tricuspid leaflets
lessons.title: Apical valve displacement
lessons.text: The inlet right ventricle between the anatomic annulus and displaced functional valve. Apical displacement atrializes the proximal inlet right ventricle while the trabecular and outlet portions form the functional right ventricle.

lessons.objective: Explain why a quiet jugular waveform can underestimate tricuspid regurgitation
lessons.title: Damped venous regurgitant signs
lessons.text: A large compliant right atrium and toneless atrialized ventricle damp low-pressure regurgitant flow. Commodious right-sided chambers and low-pressure hypokinetic regurgitation can damp the expected jugular signs.

lessons.objective: Explain temporary neonatal improvement and later recurrence
lessons.title: Changing cyanosis across life
lessons.text: A neonatal right-to-left atrial shunt can diminish as pulmonary resistance falls and reappear when abnormal right ventricular filling pressure rises. The source describes this uncommon course through changing right-sided filling conditions and interatrial shunting.

lessons.objective: Interpret a short PR interval with a delta wave
lessons.title: Preexcitation evidence
lessons.text: Preexcitation. Early delta-wave inscription supports preexcitation; a short PR interval alone can occasionally occur without a delta wave or tachycardia history.

lessons.objective: Select what echocardiography must establish
lessons.title: Defining anatomy and shunt
lessons.text: Identify a PFO or secundum defect and determine interatrial shunt direction. Color flow imaging and Doppler identify the atrial pathway and whether right-to-left shunting coexists.

case.intro: Fictional longitudinal teaching scenario: a congenital tricuspid abnormality presents differently from the newborn period to adolescence.

stages.information: A neonate has cyanosis. Echo shows apically displaced septal and posterior tricuspid leaflets with a large proximal inlet segment.
stages.prompt: How should that proximal segment be interpreted?
options: A second left atrium
An atrialized portion of the right ventricle
A separate systemic ventricle
The entire functional right ventricular outlet

Lower-body cyanosis with relative sparing of the right hand
No possible systemic desaturation

A mandatory spontaneous closure of the window

lessons.text: Falling pulmonary pressure reduces antegrade perfusion through the anomalous artery. Initially high pulmonary pressure can support antegrade flow. Its postnatal fall reduces that supply unless intercoronary perfusion becomes adequate.

An intact atrial septum

stages.information: The atrial communication is adequate. Pulmonary flow passes through a restrictive ventricular communication, and cyanosis worsens as this defect narrows.
stages.prompt: What does the narrowing represent in this arterial arrangement?
options: A new direct right AV connection
Improved pulmonary venous drainage
Relief of all outflow obstruction
Increasing subpulmonary obstruction
stages.feedback: With normally related arteries, the ventricular communication provides access to the pulmonary artery. Narrowing reduces lung flow.

stages.information: The team confirms progressively limited pulmonary flow rather than a newly restrictive atrial communication.
stages.prompt: Which explanation best accounts for deterioration despite a smaller defect?
options: Every smaller VSD is beneficial
Reduced cyanosis is guaranteed by any defect closure
Closure can remove an essential pulmonary-flow route
Arterial origins no longer matter after birth
stages.feedback: The physiologic role of a defect depends on the connections. Closure can be harmful when that defect is the required access to an outlet.

case.debrief: Trace venous entry and arterial exit separately. A VSD is not intrinsically beneficial or harmful: its effect depends on which circulation it supplies. The case teaches anatomy-based recognition rather than a procedural treatment protocol.

modules.title: The univentricular heart
modules.hook: A single pumping chamber does not imply one uniform physiology: inlet valves, outflow restriction and streaming determine the presentation.
modules.audience: Pediatric residents, cardiology trainees and clinicians studying congenital heart disease from infancy to adulthood

lessons.objective: Identify the ventricular connection used in this chapter
lessons.title: Morphologic definition
lessons.text: A morphologically defined single ventricular connection. The chapter defines the anatomy by atrial and AV connections to one main ventricular chamber, distinguishing it from other functionally single-ventricle categories.

lessons.objective: Predict contrasting cyanotic and overcirculatory presentations
lessons.title: Flow balance
lessons.text: Excess pulmonary flow with ventricular volume overload. Excess pulmonary flow produces heart failure and poor growth despite relatively mild cyanosis.

lessons.objective: Explain why single-chamber blood is not necessarily completely mixed
lessons.title: Streaming
lessons.text: Preferential streaming can direct oxygenated blood toward the aorta. The source describes partial stream separation influenced by outlet arrangement and pulmonary resistance.

lessons.objective: Identify the effect of a restrictive systemic outlet foramen
lessons.title: Outflow restriction
lessons.text: Subaortic obstruction with diversion toward the pulmonary circuit and greater volume burden. Restriction creates subaortic stenosis and may augment already excessive pulmonary flow and ventricular volume overload.

lessons.objective: Interpret a softer pulmonary stenotic murmur in context
lessons.title: Recognizing severity
lessons.text: Less blood crosses the increasingly obstructed pulmonary outlet. As stenosis increases, more flow is diverted to the systemic outlet and less traverses the pulmonary obstruction, reducing its murmur.

modules.title: Complete transposition of the great arteries
modules.hook: Parallel circulations require effective exchange; more flow through the lungs cannot help systemic oxygenation if mixing remains restricted.
modules.audience: Pediatric residents, cardiology trainees and clinicians studying congenital heart disease from infancy to adulthood
modules.prerequisites: Core cardiovascular anatomy and physiology; chapters1–2 introduce the diagnostic approach and functional murmurs.
modules.estimated_minutes_note: Planning estimate for five units and feedback; full reference reading takes longer.

lessons.objective: Distinguish complete from congenitally corrected transposition
lessons.title: Connection and circulation
lessons.text: AV concordance with ventriculoarterial discordance and parallel circuits. Complete transposition combines AV concordance and ventriculoarterial discordance, creating parallel systemic and pulmonary recirculation.

lessons.objective: Explain why atrial communication is crucial
lessons.title: Effective exchange
lessons.text: Oxygenated blood recirculates through the pulmonary circuit instead of adequately entering systemic flow. An adequate communication permits exchange between the circuits; a restrictive atrial route can leave oxygenated blood trapped in pulmonary recirculation.

lessons.objective: Avoid excluding major disease from a normal neonatal ECG
lessons.title: Normal early tests
lessons.text: A normal early ECG does not exclude the abnormal arterial connections. The chapter explicitly describes a potentially normal ECG in the first days; structural assessment remains essential.

lessons.objective: Explain lower-body oxygenation exceeding upper-body oxygenation
lessons.title: Differential cyanosis
lessons.text: More oxygenated pulmonary arterial blood enters the descending aorta beyond the left subclavian artery. Oxygenated pulmonary arterial blood can pass through the ductus to the lower body, producing less cyanotic feet.

lessons.objective: Interpret the egg-shaped silhouette as a clue rather than a complete diagnosis
lessons.title: Radiographic recognition
lessons.text: A prominent right atrium and convex enlarged left ventricle shape the silhouette. The right atrium forms the blunter right border and the enlarged left ventricle the convex left border; arterial arrangement contributes to the narrow pedicle.

case.intro: Fictional teaching scenario: a term newborn has marked persistent cyanosis.

stages.information: The early ECG is not strikingly abnormal despite persistent cyanosis.
stages.prompt: Which conclusion is justified?
options: Major structural disease remains possible and needs imaging
A normal ECG proves adequate atrial mixing
Normal electrical appearance establishes normal arterial connections
No congenital cause can present this early
stages.feedback: A neonatal ECG can initially be normal in complete transposition; it does not define arterial connections.

stages.information: Echo shows AV concordance, aorta from the right ventricle and pulmonary artery from the left ventricle.
stages.prompt: Which circulation should now guide the reasoning?
options: One normal serial circuit
Two parallel recirculating circuits
Isolated mitral obstruction in an otherwise normal circuit
A common trunk without separate arteries
stages.feedback: The ventricular-arterial discordance produces parallel circulation with dependence on communications for exchange.

stages.information: The interatrial communication is restrictive. Pulmonary flow rises, yet severe systemic hypoxemia persists.
stages.prompt: Which target directly addresses this physiologic limitation?
options: Assess and improve effective intercirculatory exchange under urgent specialist care
Interpret the unchanged saturation as proof of normal mixing
Ignore atrial communication because the ductus is visible
Assume greater pulmonary flow alone guarantees correction
stages.feedback: Adequate atrial exchange can permit oxygenated pulmonary venous blood to enter systemic circulation; simply increasing recirculation is insufficient.

case.debrief: Keep electrical findings, anatomic connections and effective exchange distinct. This staged recognition exercise explains why a severely cyanotic newborn can have a nondiagnostic early ECG and why mixing matters.

modules.title: Truncus arteriosus
modules.hook: A common trunk can produce little cyanosis while imposing a major pulmonary-flow and valve burden.
modules.audience: Pediatric residents, cardiology trainees and clinicians studying congenital heart disease from infancy to adulthood
modules.prerequisites: Core cardiovascular anatomy and physiology; chapters1–2 introduce the diagnostic approach and functional murmurs.

lessons.objective: Recognize the defining anatomy of truncus arteriosus
lessons.title: Single arterial outlet
lessons.text: Truncus arteriosus. A single great artery and single semilunar valve supply the three circulations.

lessons.objective: Differentiate the major branching patterns
lessons.title: Pulmonary branching
lessons.text: Type 1 truncus. Type 1 has a short main pulmonary artery from the trunk; separate branch ostia constitute the other grouped pattern.

lessons.objective: Interpret diminishing cyanosis with worsening heart failure
lessons.title: Cyanosis and congestion
lessons.text: Falling pulmonary resistance increases lung flow and ventricular volume load. More pulmonary flow improves systemic oxygenation but imposes volume overload and may cause severe heart failure.

lessons.objective: Explain why regurgitation can burden both ventricles
lessons.title: Truncal valve
lessons.text: Regurgitant flow is received by both ventricles and adds to their burden. The biventricular truncus permits regurgitant volume to load both ventricles, adding to existing hemodynamic stress.

lessons.objective: Connect conotruncal anatomy with immune and calcium findings
lessons.title: Associated phenotype
lessons.text: DiGeorge syndrome. The chapter describes DiGeorge-related thymic and parathyroid deficiency with truncus arteriosus.

modules.title: Congenital anomalies of vena caval connection
modules.hook: An unusual vein is not necessarily a shunt. Follow its destination and any bridging channel before predicting cyanosis.
modules.audience: Pediatric residents, cardiology trainees and clinicians studying congenital heart disease from infancy to adulthood

lessons.objective: Interpret a persistent left SVC draining to the coronary sinus
lessons.title: Benign venous route
lessons.text: The route is usually physiologically harmless despite coronary sinus dilation. Blood still reaches the right atrium through the coronary sinus, so an isolated connection need not create a physiologic derangement.

lessons.objective: Explain the effect of a nonrestrictive innominate bridge
lessons.title: Shunt direction
lessons.text: Left atrium to left SVC, across the bridge and into the right SVC. A freely communicating bridge can permit left-to-right flow from left atrium through the venous pathway to right atrium, reversing the expected cyanotic pattern.

lessons.objective: Recognize azygos continuation as an anatomic variant
lessons.title: Interrupted inferior cava
lessons.text: Azygos continuation, which can be physiologically insignificant in isolation. The interrupted inferior caval flow continues through a dilated azygos system to the right SVC; isolated cases need not cause a shunt.

lessons.objective: Use coronary sinus dilation to direct venous imaging
lessons.title: Coronary sinus clue
lessons.text: Persistent left superior vena cava. An unexpectedly enlarged coronary sinus can be the clue to an unsuspected left SVC; color and contrast studies define the route.

lessons.objective: Recognize a caval-to-left atrial shunt pattern
lessons.title: Cyanosis without RV overload
lessons.text: Right-heart flow is normal or reduced because some systemic venous blood bypasses it. Anomalous caval return bypasses the right heart, unlike lesions with major RV pressure or volume overload.

modules.title: Congenital pulmonary arteriovenous fistula
modules.hook: Cyanosis with a normal-sized heart and a peripheral lung vascular lesion suggests a shunt outside the cardiac chambers.
modules.audience: Pediatric residents, cardiology trainees and clinicians studying congenital heart disease from infancy to adulthood
modules.prerequisites: Core cardiovascular anatomy and physiology; chapters1–2 introduce the diagnostic approach and functional murmurs.
modules.estimated_minutes_note: Planning estimate for five units and feedback; full reference reading takes longer.

lessons.objective: Explain hypoxemia with limited chamber loading
lessons.title: Bypassing gas exchange
lessons.text: Blood bypasses gas exchange while flow through uninvolved lung may fall reciprocally. The right-to-left intrapulmonary route bypasses the capillary bed; redistribution can limit the net increase in ventricular flow.

lessons.objective: Recognize hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia
lessons.title: Associated vasculopathy
lessons.text: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia. The source describes an autosomal dominant vasculopathy with mucocutaneous bleeding and visceral arteriovenous malformations.

lessons.objective: Use peripheral and respiratory features of a fistulous murmur
lessons.title: Auscultatory localization
lessons.text: A peripheral pulmonary fistula can generate a localized flow murmur. Peripheral fistulae transmit sounds to the overlying chest wall; inspiratory flow and reduced compression may increase audibility.

lessons.objective: Interpret delayed left-heart bubbles as a localization clue
lessons.title: Delayed contrast
lessons.text: A pulmonary right-to-left shunt. The chapter describes delayed appearance beyond three cycles as usually indicating pulmonary shunting; the timing is a clue interpreted with anatomy.

lessons.objective: Connect pulmonary bypass with embolic and infectious complications
lessons.title: Neurologic risk
lessons.text: Paradoxical embolism, stroke and brain abscess. The shunt bypasses the pulmonary filter; the source highlights embolic events and brain abscess.

case.intro: Fictional teaching scenario: a young adult has cyanosis, recurrent epistaxis and a lung opacity.

stages.information: A routine chest film shows a lower-lobe rounded opacity with channels extending toward the hilum. The cardiac silhouette is normal.
stages.prompt: What should be investigated before assuming a nonvascular lung nodule?
options: Only an intracardiac ventricular defect
A normal pulmonary finding requiring no further assessment
A pulmonary vascular fistulous communication
Only an isolated aortic valve lesion
stages.feedback: The vascular channels and location support consideration of a pulmonary fistula even with a normal-sized heart.

stages.information: Examination identifies small lip and oral telangiectases; the patient’s parent has recurrent nosebleeds.
stages.prompt: Which associated diagnosis is most coherent?
options: Congenital complete heart block
Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia
A purely acquired aortic dissection
An isolated pulmonary valve malformation
stages.feedback: Familial epistaxis, mucocutaneous lesions and pulmonary AV malformations fit the inherited vasculopathy described.

stages.information: Venous contrast imaging supports an intrapulmonary right-to-left shunt. Symptoms have been modest for years.
stages.prompt: Which risk must remain part of assessment and counseling?
options: Paradoxical embolism and brain abscess
Only harmless discoloration
No complications are possible with a normal silhouette
Only eventual mitral stenosis
stages.feedback: The bypass permits embolic and infectious complications despite a modest circulatory load.

case.debrief: Locate the shunt rather than assuming all cyanosis is intracardiac. The lung opacity, vascular channels, contrast passage and family phenotype supply complementary evidence; quiet hemodynamics do not equal absence of risk.

modules.title: Hypoplastic left heart
modules.hook: A newborn can have profound systemic hypoperfusion with little murmur. Trace ductal systemic supply, coronary supply and left atrial escape.
modules.audience: Pediatric residents, cardiology trainees and clinicians studying congenital heart disease from infancy to adulthood
modules.prerequisites: Core cardiovascular anatomy and physiology; chapters1–2 introduce the diagnostic approach and functional murmurs.

lessons.objective: Trace systemic and coronary supply when the aortic valve is atretic
lessons.title: Systemic route
lessons.text: Right ventricle through pulmonary trunk, ductus and descending aorta. The pulmonary artery/ductus/descending aortic continuity provides systemic flow; retrograde flow supplies the small ascending aorta and coronary origins.

lessons.objective: Explain systemic and myocardial compromise during ductal constriction
lessons.title: Ductal deterioration
lessons.text: Reduced systemic and retrograde coronary perfusion impairs output and RV function. The ductus supports systemic and coronary supply; constriction compromises both and can worsen the sole pumping ventricle.

lessons.objective: Distinguish a higher saturation from better systemic perfusion
lessons.title: Oxygen delivery
lessons.text: Flow is preferentially diverted to the lungs at the expense of systemic output. The right ventricle supplies both beds; increasing lung flow can improve mixing saturation while reducing systemic blood flow.

lessons.objective: Recognize severe disease despite an absent murmur
lessons.title: Quiet auscultation
lessons.text: A severe ductal-dependent left-heart lesion remains possible. The source emphasizes unimpressive auscultation despite dramatic illness; aortic atresia leaves a single pulmonary closure sound.

lessons.objective: Explain the importance of the interatrial communication
lessons.title: Atrial exit
lessons.text: Pulmonary venous return encounters an obstructed left atrium. The left atrium needs an alternative exit when mitral inflow is severely limited; atrial restriction compromises that exit and promotes congestion.

case.intro: Fictional teaching scenario: a newborn develops circulatory collapse during the first days of life.

stages.information: The baby is listless and tachypneic with poor perfusion. A loud single second sound and RV impulse are present, but no major murmur.
stages.prompt: Which interpretation avoids a recognition error?
options: A normal aortic outlet is established by the RV impulse
No murmur rules out critical structural disease
The single sound proves two normal semilunar valves
Critical congenital disease remains possible despite quiet auscultation
stages.feedback: The source describes severe left-heart hypoplasia with little or no murmur despite major illness.

stages.information: Echo identifies aortic atresia, a hypoplastic left ventricle and ductal supply to the systemic circulation.
stages.prompt: What does ductal constriction threaten?
options: Only a harmless flow murmur
Systemic and retrograde coronary perfusion
An already normal LV-to-aorta route
Only coronary venous return
stages.feedback: The ductus supplies the descending aorta and retrograde arch/ascending aortic route to the coronary arteries.

stages.information: With a patent ductus and adequate atrial communication, pulmonary flow increases. Saturation rises, but peripheral perfusion worsens.
stages.prompt: What explains this apparent contradiction?
options: A saturation rise excludes circulatory imbalance
Higher saturation guarantees adequate systemic delivery
Pulmonary flow can increase at the expense of systemic output
The left ventricle has necessarily normalized
stages.feedback: A shared RV output must be balanced between the two circulations; oxygen saturation does not measure systemic flow.

case.debrief: Recognize the lesion even when auscultation is quiet, trace coronary and systemic supply, then interpret saturation together with perfusion. The scenario explains physiology and does not prescribe an isolated oxygen or ventilation target.

modules.title: Congenital anomalies of the coronary circulation
modules.hook: A coronary anomaly needs a route map: origin alone is less informative than the ostium, proximal course, branches and surrounding anatomy.

lessons.objective: Identify the coronary feature most relevant to risk assessment
lessons.title: Origin versus course
lessons.text: Whether its course is anterior, retroaortic, interarterial or intramyocardial. The source emphasizes that the route relative to the great arteries can be more important than the ectopic origin itself.

lessons.objective: Recognize the source-described high-risk left coronary arrangement
lessons.title: Higher-risk anatomy
lessons.text: Left main from the right sinus passing between aorta and RV outflow tract. The source identifies the left main or major left branch passing between the aorta and RV outflow tract as particularly concerning; ostial shape and exercise also affect risk.

lessons.objective: Distinguish separate left coronary ostia from left main atresia
lessons.title: Absent versus atretic
lessons.text: Absence of a common left main trunk, generally functionally benign. Separate patent LAD and circumflex origins are different from a blind or imperforate left main origin.

lessons.objective: Recognize a coronary crossing the RV outflow tract
lessons.title: Surgical relevance
lessons.text: It may create major surgical risk despite little baseline physiologic effect. A coronary crossing the outflow tract can be endangered during intervention even when its resting physiologic effect is small.

lessons.objective: Explain survival with congenital left main atresia
lessons.title: Collateral dependence
lessons.text: Adequate channels from a normally arising right coronary artery. Survival depends on adequate connections from the right coronary artery to the distal left system; presentation can span infancy to adulthood.
